title: Crane Up
description: A crane shot lifts the camera on a jib or Technocrane, often easing backward at the same time, so the frame climbs from a human scale into a wider view of the location. Height change is the point, and a little boom-out keeps the subject from sliding off the bottom of the frame.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: A crane-up starts at human height and leaves it. The person stays in frame, then the rooftops, then the city.
By the end, the figure is one dark coat in a much larger night. Use it when the scene needs to end, or when a private moment has to admit the world that contains it.
A tilt up only changes the angle. A crane changes the map.
Do not use it as decoration on every wide. If nothing new appears as the camera climbs, the move is empty.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: The operator rides or remote-heads a crane. The arm can be a few feet (a jib) or tens of feet (a Technocrane).

Keep a foreground anchor visible during the rise so the newly revealed scale has a reference. Prompt crane up and slightly back, name the start (shoulder height, waist, close-up), and name the reveal (rooftops, canyon, overpass).
If you only write camera goes up, you often get a tilt or a cheap zoom.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it to end a scene, reveal a city, or turn a person into landscape. Concrete beat: a woman on a wet roof, then the square below takes the frame.
Do not crane up if the last frame shows nothing the first frame did not already imply.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: A Tilt Up rotates on a fixed tripod. A Jib Shot is the short-arm version of this family.
An Aerial Pullback continues until geography wins completely from helicopter or high-drone height. A Pull Out stays at eye height and only retreats.
Crane Down arrives at a face instead of leaving one.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The opening of Touch of Evil treats the crane as a long sentence through a border town. The wounded-field pullaway in Gone with the Wind turns a person into a statistic of war.
La La Land lets hillside and dock cranes sit romance in a real city. The Player opens on studio-lot crane choreography.
Grammar, not frames to copy.
Gone with the Wind 1939Scarlett crosses the Atlanta station area as the view rises over wounded soldiers.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Majestic crane up from [Subject], camera rising and easing backward on a Technocrane, the individual becoming one figure inside a vast environment, golden or blue-hour air, 35mm Signature Prime. For motion: the camera cranes smoothly upward and slightly backward from shoulder height, rising above [Subject] to reveal the true surrounding scale.
Slow 6-second crane up.

Begin at eye level beside one volunteer carrying water. Crane upward and backward to reveal hundreds of orderly relief tents across a dry valley. One continuous shot; the volunteer becomes small but remains trackable. Realistic scale and coherent tent spacing, no sudden aerial cut.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is a Tilt Up or a cut from close-up to aerial. The tell is no parallax, or a jump in scale with no continuous ascent.
The fix: physical rise plus a little boom-out, a visible foreground anchor, continuity of the figure all the way up.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Crane Up in film?
It is a physical lift of the camera on a jib or crane, often easing back, so a human-scale frame becomes a wider view of the place.
Crane Up vs Tilt Up
A tilt rotates the camera on a fixed tripod. A crane physically moves the camera through space, so foreground, mid-ground, and background change in parallax.
When should I use Crane Up?
When a scene should close, or a private beat must admit the city, crowd, or land that contains it. Do not use it if the climb reveals nothing new.
How do I prompt Crane Up for AI image or video?
Name starting height, crane up and slightly back, and what is revealed. Example: camera cranes up and slightly back from shoulder height, revealing rooftops and the city beyond.
